paras: The threatened lynching at the McDonald colliery was an averted lynching of an unnamed Black striker in Fayette County, West Virginia, on June 3, 1903, after a shot he fired killed a company guard, William Mann. He was taken from a crowd of 'angry men' to the county jail, and two West Virginia papers reported the case as an episode of the New River coal strike.

In early June 1903 strikers and colliery guards in the New River coal field were in conflict, and the Huntington Advertiser called this shooting the 'second clash' between them. Mann was a guard employed by the McDonald Coal Company, whose colliery stood on Loup creek.

According to a Fayette dispatch, guards tried to arrest a Black striker, who resisted and then drew a revolver and fired at the guard arresting him. The bullet missed that man and struck Mann, who was standing close by and died almost at once. In the 'great excitement' that followed, it looked for a time as if the striker would be lynched. He was instead 'rescued from the hands of the angry men' and taken to the county jail, where he was still held on June 4.
Neither report names the jailed man, and no report of an inquest, indictment or trial was found in the coverage.

The Huntington Advertiser ran a special from Fayette on its front page on June 4 under a headline centered on the guard: 'Second Clash with Strikers Results in the Death of William Mann, Coal Company's Guard.' Six days later the Ceredo Advance reduced the story to three sentences among its 'State News Pick-ups', calling the killing 'an accident' and saying the man was jailed 'to avoid a possible lynching'. No coverage of the episode was found in the Black press.

The two accounts differ on whom the striker meant to shoot: the Fayette dispatch says the guard who was arresting him, while the Ceredo Advance says a man named Dixon. Neither paper says whether Dixon was the arresting guard; both agree Mann was not the intended target.

reader.title: Threatened lynching at the McDonald colliery, Fayette County, West Virginia
bases: Both reports describe a Black striker whom a crowd was expected to lynch after a guard was killed, and who was taken to the county jail instead; no injury to him is reported, so this was a threatened, not a completed, lynching (A1, A2).

Two white papers with different details (A1's Fayette special; A2's Loup creek item naming Dixon) agree that a Black striker resisting arrest killed guard William Mann and was jailed to save him from lynching (A1, A2).

accounts.label: Fayette special to the Huntington Advertiser
accounts.gist: Guards tried to arrest a Black striker, who drew a revolver and fired at the guard arresting him; the bullet missed and killed Mann. Amid 'great excitement' he nearly was lynched but was rescued from the 'angry men' and jailed.

accounts.label: State news roundup
accounts.gist: A Black miner resisting arrest at the McDonald colliery on Loup creek killed guard Mann by accident while firing at a man named Dixon, and was taken to the county jail to avoid a possible lynching.

framing.detail: The Huntington Advertiser headlined it 'SECOND CLASH WITH STRIKERS RESULTS IN THE DEATH OF WILLIAM MANN, COAL COMPANY'S GUARD', centering the guard's death and reporting the near-lynching without comment.
The Ceredo Advance ran a three-sentence item among state briefs, calling the killing 'an accident' and noting the jailing 'to avoid a possible lynching'.

conflicts.note: The versions may be compatible if Dixon was the arresting guard, but neither paper says so; both agree the bullet that killed Mann was meant for someone else.
